title: Ziryab the musician
hookLine: a musician from Baghdad who brought new music, food and fashion to Cordoba

cards: Soup first. Then the meat. Then something sweet to finish.
A meal in courses, on a table that might have glass on it instead of gold. In the stories of al-Andalus, that order at dinner is credited to one man, and he wasn't a cook.

He was a singer from Baghdad with an oud on his back. People called him Ziryab. He came west to Cordoba, and the reports say the city started eating, dressing and even cutting its hair the way he did.

teach.b: The story comes mostly through the historian al-Maqqari, gathering older accounts. In Baghdad, Ziryab studied music under a well-known master, Ishaq al-Mawsili. The student became too good.
When he sang before the caliph, his teacher grew jealous and told him, in effect, to leave or face trouble.

teach.h: A NEW LIFE AT CORDOBA'S COURT.
teach.b: So Ziryab went west, and in Cordoba the emir Abd al-Rahman the Second welcomed him to his court. Then the reports, a long list.

teach.h: A STRING, A QUILL, A MEAL IN COURSES.
teach.b: He added a string to the oud. He played with a plectrum made from an eagle's quill instead of wood. He opened a school of music.

And off the stage: meals in courses, glass vessels on the table, clothes changed with the seasons, a new way to wear the hair. Historians read that list carefully; some of it may be praise piled on a well-known name.
But the picture of a court learning taste from one gifted person holds together. Why spend a day on a singer?
Partly because Muslim scholars differ over music: some permit instruments, some don't, and others draw lines in between. And partly for a hadith.
Sahih Muslim records that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, warned against pride, and a man asked: what if someone likes his clothes fine and his sandals good?

teach.h: GOD IS BEAUTIFUL AND LOVES BEAUTY.
teach.b: The answer, in substance: God is beautiful and loves beauty; pride is rejecting the truth and looking down on people. Care for how things look was never the problem. Contempt was.
That fits the week so far: ilm, Tariq's mountain, Cordoba and its mosque, a caliph, a man with wings, and now a man with manners.

how: Ziryab is remembered in histories of al-Andalus as a court musician and a setter of taste; Muslim scholars hold a range of views on music and instruments, from permitting them to forbidding them.

the emir who welcomed a musician to his Cordoba court

games.q: you're Ziryab in Baghdad. you've just sung well before the caliph, and your own teacher, jealous, tells you to leave or face trouble. what do you do?
o: stay and fight for your place at court.
leave Baghdad and take your music west.
games.why: by al-Maqqari's account he left, and in Cordoba the emir Abd al-Rahman the Second took him in. the teacher's jealousy sent the music to Spain.

practice: Think of one dish you love that someone close to you has never had, and picture it in order: what goes in first, how it smells, how it looks on the plate. Then picture the person you'd share it with.
If you pray, give thanks for the food in the words you already know; if you don't, simply notice the gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Ziryab. The singer from Baghdad who, by the reports, taught Cordoba new music, new meals and new manners. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the oud, the lute Ziryab played.

carryVoice: Your line: music and manners. A clean plate and a quiet minute count too. See you tomorrow.
